analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal tax breaks and royalty relief for the largest oil companies, dedicating the savings to deficit reduction.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take away five long-standing tax breaks that apply only to the biggest oil companies — companies with over $1 billion in annual revenue and at least 500,000 barrels of daily oil production — and would end royalty relief that lets some Gulf of Mexico offshore drillers pay less (or nothing) for oil and gas taken from federal waters. Every dollar saved would go toward reducing the federal deficit and debt. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in the form of a slightly smaller federal deficit, since the bill dedicates all revenue raised to deficit and debt reduction [S2]. Small and mid-sized oil and gas producers would also gain a modest competitive edge, because the bill's tax changes apply only to the largest integrated companies [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates or limits five tax benefits available only to 'major integrated oil companies,' including the domestic production deduction, intangible drilling cost expensing, and percentage depletion for oil and gas wells [S2].
It tightens the foreign tax credit for oil companies that pay levies to foreign governments in exchange for drilling rights, closing a deduction for payments that are not truly income taxes [S2].

It repeals royalty relief under the Energy Policy Act of 2005 that suspended royalties for deep gas in shallow Gulf waters and deep-water oil and gas production in parts of the Gulf of Mexico, so those drillers would pay the government for what they extract from federal waters [S2].
All net savings must be deposited in the Treasury and used to reduce the federal deficit or debt [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest oil companies — those with over $1 billion in gross receipts and at least 500,000 barrels of daily worldwide production — would pay billions more in taxes, and offshore Gulf drillers would pay royalties that had been suspended. Some of the added cost could eventually reach consumers through fuel prices, though the bill targeted only the largest firms [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The benefits are diffuse: the savings go to deficit reduction rather than to any visible improvement in taxpayers' daily lives, so few people would feel a direct gain [S3].

Raising costs for the largest oil producers could marginally increase fuel and energy prices, a cost that supporters would have to acknowledge even though the burden falls only on companies above a large size threshold [S2].
Removing drilling-cost deductions and royalty relief could modestly discourage domestic exploration and production in the Gulf of Mexico [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted, well-defined revenue measure: it narrows tax preferences that apply only to the very largest oil companies and routes every dollar to deficit reduction, so the direct cost to ordinary people is minimal and possibly zero. The main honest objection is that energy prices could tick up slightly and that deficit reduction is an invisible benefit. On balance, the benefits to taxpayers outweigh the costs, though no independent cost estimate was ever published because the bill never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez introduced the bill on July 30, 2015, joined by 18 Democratic cosponsors, all members of the Senate Democratic caucus [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance — the only action the bill ever received [S5].
The Finance Committee held no markup or hearing on the bill, and the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major integrated oil companies, which kept all five tax breaks and Gulf of Mexico royalty relief intact for the rest of the Congress, and federal taxpayers lost the revenue the bill would have raised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big oil companies kept their tax breaks

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 18 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Markey, Whitehouse, Schumer, Durbin, and Boxer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or hearing on the bill after it was referred, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee and Senate took no action on the bill; there is no record of any Republican supporting it.

industries.note: The bill strips five tax preferences available only to companies with over $1 billion in receipts and 500,000 barrels of daily production, and tightens their foreign tax credit claims. Their continued enjoyment of these breaks costs the Treasury revenue that would otherwise reduce the deficit. Since the bill died, they keep every break.

industries.industry: Gulf of Mexico offshore oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill repeals royalty relief from the Energy Policy Act of 2005 that suspended royalties for deep-water and shallow-water deep gas production in the Gulf, meaning drillers would pay the government for resources taken from federal waters. With the bill dead, royalty relief remains available.

industries.industry: Smaller and independent oil and gas producers
industries.note: Because the new limits apply only to 'major integrated oil companies' above a large size threshold, smaller producers are untouched and would face slightly less advantaged large-firm competitors. The bill's death leaves the status quo in place.
